newsitem.title: UK: Compromise ends UK lottery pay row.
newsitem.headline: Compromise ends UK lottery pay row.

text.p: Executives from British lottery operator Camelot Group Plc agreed on Friday to give some of their future bonuses to charity in a concession that ended a bitter row with the government.

The new Labour government expressed outrage last week when it emerged that bonus payments had inflated Camelot's wage bill by 40 percent to 2.3 million pounds ($3.7 million) while the sum the lottery raised for good causes fell.

Chris Smith, the minister responsible for the lottery, had called for some of the bonuses to be handed over to charity. A number of Camelot executives had reportedly been on the verge of resigning over the row.
In a compromise deal, Camelot's main executives have agreed to contribute part of forthcoming long-term bonus entitlements to a joint charity fund.
Camelot itself will give to charity a sum equivalent to the one million pounds of bonuses paid to its directors in the last financial year.
"I now regard the matter as closed and will press on with work to make the national lottery more a people's lottery," Smith said in a statement.

Smith said the government would next month publish details of plans to plough one billion pounds of lottery funds into health and education projects over the next five years. The money is expected to come from a second midweek draw launched earlier this year.
The government will also outline its plans to give the lottery to a non-profit operator when Camelot's licence expires in 2001.
Camelot has also agreed to pay interest from undistributed prize money to good causes rather than keeping the money. It said this could amount to 24 million pounds over the next four years.
"The national lottery is a great success; I am a strong supporter of it," Smith added.
Launched in 1994, the lottery is played regularly by some 30 million Britons who dream of winning jackpots which can top 10 million pounds.
But its critics have labelled the lottery a "tax on the poor" and attacked Camelot for its big profits and "fat cat" executive salaries.
Camelot counters by arguing that it has raised billions of pounds for charities, sports and the arts while taking a profit after tax of less than a penny in the pound.
The lottery operator, owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, De La Rue Plc, GTECH UK, Racal Electronics and ICL, is to discuss with the government how a non-profit operator might work.
Smith said in a letter to Camelot chairman Sir George Russell that Camelot would be considered as a candidate to run the reformed lottery when its licence expires.
Russell told Smith that contributions paid by executives to the joint charity fund would be a personal matter but monitored by non-executive directors. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
